questions.question: Describe the three levels of healthcare and explain why primary healthcare is so important.
questions.expected_answer: Primary: first contact - community health workers, mobile clinics, clinics and community health centres (mainly nurses) providing immunisation, antenatal and child care, family planning, treatment of common illness, HIV/TB care and health education. Secondary: district and regional hospitals (operations, complicated births). Tertiary: large specialist hospitals (e.g. Chris Hani Baragwanath, Groote Schuur). Primary healthcare reaches most people cheaply and prevents and treats the common causes of death, so it lowers death rates most (Alma-Ata 1978).

questions.question: Explain how healthcare lowers infant and child mortality.
questions.expected_answer: Antenatal care and skilled birth attendants make pregnancy and birth safer; the Road to Health booklet and weighing detect malnutrition; free immunisation (BCG, measles, polio, rotavirus, pneumococcal) prevents killer diseases; breastfeeding, ORS, vitamin A, deworming, nets and prompt pneumonia treatment save lives; prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission reduced infections to below 1% of births.

questions.question: How does healthcare affect birth rates, and what challenges does South African healthcare face?
questions.expected_answer: Free family planning and contraception at clinics, together with education of girls, let people choose family size; when child survival improves, parents choose fewer children (demographic transition) - SA fertility fell from about 6 to about 2.3. Challenges: about 80% depend on an overstretched public system while most doctors are private; queues, staff shortages, stock-outs; rural shortages; growing lifestyle diseases; violence and road accidents; NHI debate.
